claims.text: What the image looks like Radiopaque stone along ureter, hydroureter → nephrolithiasis (Ca-oxalate ~80% opaque)
claims.quote: Radiopaque stone along ureter, hydroureter Nephrolithiasis (Ca-oxalate ~80% opaque)

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Calcifications: aorta (AAA), phleboliths, renal/ureteral stones, gallstones, pancreatic, appendicolith
claims.quote: Calcifications: aorta (AAA), phleboliths, renal/ureteral stones, gallstones (~10-15% radiopaque), pancreatic, appendicolith.

claims.text: Most calculi show on a radiograph, but more definitive imaging is still needed, so the radiograph can be skipped except in some suspected recurrent stones
claims.quote: Although most urinary calculi can be visualized on radiograph, more definitive imaging is still needed regardless of their presence, so taking a radiograph can be avoided except in some patients with suspected recurrent calculi.

claims.text: Noncontrast CT is the preferred initial study in most patients: it shows the stone’s location and the degree of obstruction, and may reveal other causes of pain (eg, aortic aneurysm)
claims.quote: Noncontrast CT is the preferred initial imaging study in most patients. This study can detect the location of a calculus as well as the degree of obstruction. Moreover, CT may also reveal other causes of the pain (eg, aortic aneurysm).

claims.text: Ultrasound and excretory urography can show calculi and hydronephrosis (generally used when CT is unavailable); ultrasound is less sensitive for small or ureteral stones without hydronephrosis
claims.quote: Both renal ultrasonography and excretory urography (previously called intravenous urography or intravenous pyelography) can identify calculi and hydronephrosis. However, ultrasonography is less sensitive for small or ureteral calculi in patients without hydronephrosis, and excretory urography is time-consuming and exposes the patient to the risk of IV contrast agents. These studies are generally used when CT is unavailable.

claims.text: CT: hyperdense calculus in ureter; hydroureter, hydronephrosis, perinephric stranding → ureterolithiasis
claims.quote: Hyperdense calculus in ureter; hydroureter, hydronephrosis, perinephric stranding Ureterolithiasis

claims.text: Causes In the US, approximately 85% are calcium (mainly calcium oxalate); 5 to 10% uric acid, 1 to 2% cystine, 5 to 15% struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate)
claims.quote: Approximately 85% of calculi in the United States are composed of calcium, mainly calcium oxalate (see table ); 5 to 10% are composed of uric acid, 1 to 2% of cystine; and 5 to 15% of magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite).

claims.text: Struvite (infection) stones indicate UTI with urea-splitting bacteria (eg, Proteus, Klebsiella) and must be removed entirely
claims.quote: Magnesium ammonium phosphate calculi (struvite, infection calculi) indicate the presence of urinary tract infection caused by urea-splitting bacteria (eg, Proteus species, Klebsiella species). These calculi must be treated as infected foreign bodies and removed in their entirety.

claims.text: Typically a stone that lodges is > 5 mm; stones ≤ 5 mm are more likely to pass spontaneously
claims.quote: Typically, a calculus that becomes lodged has a diameter > 5 mm, whereas calculi ≤ 5 mm are more likely to pass spontaneously.

claims.text: Symptoms Severe pain, often with nausea and vomiting, usually when a stone enters the ureter and obstructs; gross hematuria occurs, but not in all patients
claims.quote: Severe pain, often accompanied by nausea and vomiting, usually occurs when calculi pass into the ureter and cause acute obstruction. Gross hematuria also occurs, but not in all patients with urinary tract stones.

claims.text: Renal colic: variable intensity but typically excruciating and intermittent, often cyclic, lasting 20 to 60 minutes; flank pain radiating across the abdomen suggests upper ureter/renal pelvis obstruction; radiation into the genital region suggests lower ureter
claims.quote: Pain (renal colic) is of variable intensity but is typically excruciating and intermittent, often occurs cyclically, and lasts 20 to 60 minutes. Nausea and vomiting are common. Pain in the flank or kidney area that radiates across the abdomen suggests upper ureteral or renal pelvic obstruction. Pain that radiates along the course of the ureter into the genital region suggests lower ureteral obstruction.

claims.text: Patients may be unable to lie still (pacing, writhing); costovertebral angle tenderness may be present, but without peritoneal signs
claims.quote: Patients with renal colic may be unable to lie still and may pace, writhe, or constantly shift position. The abdomen may be somewhat tender on the affected side as palpation increases pressure in the already-distended kidney (costovertebral angle tenderness), but without peritoneal signs (guarding, rebound, rigidity).

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: non-contrast CT confirms; ≤ 5 mm pass spontaneously
claims.quote: Non-contrast CT confirms; ≤5 mm pass spontaneously

claims.text: Her chart (CT, ureterolithiasis): tamsulosin; lithotripsy / ureteroscopy if >10 mm or obstructing
claims.quote: Tamsulosin; lithotripsy / ureteroscopy if >10 mm or obstructing

claims.text: Renal colic: opioids (morphine; fentanyl for rapid onset) or ketorolac (rapid, nonsedating); an antiemetic (eg, ondansetron) for persistent vomiting
claims.quote: Renal colic may be relieved with opioids, such as morphine and, for a rapid onset, fentanyl. Ketorolac is rapidly effective and nonsedating. Vomiting usually resolves as pain decreases, but persistent vomiting can be treated with an antiemetic (eg, ondansetron).

claims.text: Stones < 1 cm with no infection or obstruction, pain controlled and liquids tolerated: can go home on analgesics and alpha-blockers (eg, tamsulosin) to help passage
claims.quote: Patients with calculi < 1 cm in diameter who have no infection or obstruction, whose pain is controlled with analgesics, and who can tolerate liquids can be treated at home with analgesics and alpha-receptor blockers (eg, tamsulosin) to facilitate calculus passage.

claims.text: Calculi not passed within 6 to 8 weeks typically require removal; with suspected infection and obstruction, first relieve the obstruction as soon as possible (ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy) and treat the infection, then remove the calculi once feasible
claims.quote: Calculi that have not passed within 6 to 8 weeks typically require removal. In patients with suspected infection and obstruction, initial treatment is relief of obstruction as soon as possible with a cystoscopically placed ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy tube and treatment of the infection, followed by removal of calculi once feasible.

claims.text: Symptomatic calculi < 1 cm in the renal collecting system or proximal ureter: shock wave lithotripsy is a reasonable first option; larger calculi or failed shock wave lithotripsy: ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy is usually used
claims.quote: For symptomatic calculi < 1 cm in diameter in the renal collecting system or proximal ureter, shock wave lithotripsy is a reasonable first option for therapy. For larger calculi or if shock wave lithotripsy is unsuccessful, ureteroscopy (performed in a retrograde fashion) with holmium or thulium laser lithotripsy is usually used.

claims.text: Midureteral calculi: ureteroscopy with holmium laser lithotripsy is usually the treatment of choice (shock wave lithotripsy is an alternative); distal ureteral calculi: ureteroscopy is considered by many to be the procedure of choice (shock wave lithotripsy can also be used)
claims.quote: For midureteral calculi, ureteroscopy with holmium laser lithotripsy is usually the treatment of choice. Shock wave lithotripsy is an alternative. For distal ureteral calculi, endoscopic techniques (ureteroscopy), such as direct removal and use of intracorporeal lithotripsy (eg, holmium or thulium laser, pneumatic), are considered by many to be the procedures of choice. Shock wave lithotripsy can also be used.

claims.text: Remove calculi that cause infection or persist (endoscopically)
claims.quote: Give analgesics and other medications to facilitate calculus passage (eg, alpha-receptor blockers) acutely, and remove calculi that cause infection or persist endoscopically.

claims.text: Prevent recurrence by stone composition: thiazides, potassium citrate, more fluid, less dietary animal protein
claims.quote: Decrease the risk of subsequent calculus formation by treating with thiazide diuretics, potassium citrate, increased fluid intake, and decreased dietary animal protein, depending on calculus composition.
